title: Raseokan / Ratiocan of Matinecock
summary: Raseokan, also written Raseocan, Ratiocan, Rasaocume, Rashaokan, Resorokon, Aseton, Asiapum, or Asharoken in different records and later histories, was a seventeenth-century Matinecock sagamore associated with the North Shore around Huntington, Eaton's Neck, Cold Spring Harbor, Northport, Lloyd Neck, and Oyster Bay.
content:
Raseokan, also recorded under several spellings including Ratiocan, was a seventeenth-century Matinecock sagamore associated with the North Shore from Huntington and Eaton's Neck to Oyster Bay. Colonial records document his leadership from 1646 through 1656, but the cited sources do not establish his birth or death dates.

Colonial deeds preserve only fragments of his life, but those fragments show a leader working in a period of intense pressure from English settlement.13

Historical Context

In 1646, a deed recorded Resorokon, sagamore of Ketanomocke, granting land at Eaton's Neck to Theophilus Eaton of New Haven.2

On April 2, 1653, Raseokan appears as sagamore of Matinecock in the First Purchase of Huntington, which described bounds from Cold Spring Harbor toward Northport.3

On September 20, 1654, Ratiocan, identified as sagamore of Cow Harbor, sold Caumsett, now Lloyd Neck, to Samuel Mayo.4

In July 1656, Asharoken appears in the Eastern Purchase of Huntington, another record that should remain distinct from the earlier Caumsett transaction.5

These records were written by colonial authorities and purchasers, not by Raseokan in his own voice.1

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.
  2. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, pp. 37-38, 113, 149.
  3. Cold Spring Harbor Soundings, 1953, First Purchase deed transcription.
  4. Tales of Old Lloyd Harbor, deed transcription for September 20, 1654.
  5. Brewster-Walker master research notes preserving the July 1656 Eastern Purchase transcription, p. 51.
why_this_matters: Raseokan / Ratiocan offers a glimpse of Matinecock leadership through the surviving record of North Shore land negotiations, while also showing the limits of colonial documents that preserve transactions more fully than personal lives.
